item.title: Amazon's Plan to Index the World's Online Shopping Data
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Amazon is considering a "World Product Graph" that would index information about products sold across the internet in an effort to keep shoppers and AI agents from turning to Google, Reddit or other sources for product research. The proposed database could also improve Amazon's AI shopping assistant by addressing inaccurate or incomplete answers and allowing it to use cheaper models.
"Amazon cannot be the go-destination for every shopping mission if customers must leave to research product relationships on Google, brand websites, and review sites," according to an internal Amazon document. "These answers exist, but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums." Reuters could not determine if or when this plan may be implemented, though the document, written like a press release, has an aspirational future release date of October 1, 2027.
Amazon said in a statement: "Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn't necessarily reflect our current plans. We're constantly working on new ideas and technologies to make Amazon's product catalog comprehensive, accurate, and helpful for customers."

item.title: Windows 0-Day Dropped By Disgruntled Researcher Hands Hackers System Rights
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a "general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode." By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
[...] Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there's a catch, he said. "The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems," he explained. "That is, you can't just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work." For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode value must be 0 or 1." Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement. Microsoft said in a statement that it was investigating the vulnerability and had no evidence it was being exploited in the wild. The company also said Defender blocks potential exploitation attempts.

item.title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop for All Aircraft [UPDATE]
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Longtime Slashdot readers cold fjord and sinij share news that the FAA grounded flights nationwide after a communications failure disrupted air traffic control centers across the country. By Friday evening, the outage had resulted in nearly 5,000 flight cancellations and roughly 10,000 delays, with no timeline for restoring normal operations. Rumors are swirling that this could be related to the FAA's newly deployed SMART AI system or Microsoft's recent global outage, but both the agency and Microsoft said they had no indication that their technology was responsible. Business Insider reports: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said just after 4:15 pm. Eastern time that the nationwide flight traffic halt came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he said in a post on X. The outage comes the same week as the FAA deployed SMART, a new AI tool to help air traffic control. ASI, the company that makes the SMART system for the FAA, said that Friday's issues weren't "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a press conference Friday, when asked if the AI system might be related to the outage: "That's what we're looking at." Microsoft, which faced massive issues across its services this week, also said that it had "no indication" the ground stop was related to any Microsoft services. Meanwhile, the FAA said that the ground stop was due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." UPDATE 1:33 UTC: Secretary Mullin and Secretary Duffy are currently briefing members of the press on the issue.
UPDATE 1:46 UTC: The FAA has lifted the nationwide ground stop after more than four hours. Officials said the disruption appears to have stemmed from a network router issue that cascaded nationwide, with no evidence of a cyberattack or connection to Microsoft's recent outage. Airlines warned that disruptions could continue in Saturday.

item.title: SpaceX Falls Short of Historic Double Starship Catch
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX's 15th Starship test flight successfully reached orbit Friday, but its historic attempt to catch both stages at the launch tower was derailed when the Super Heavy booster malfunctioned, forcing controllers to abort its return before it exploded after splashing down in the Gulf of Mexico. The upper-stage Starship did, however, successfully deploy 26 Starlink satellites and is scheduled to complete 15 orbits before attempting an unprecedented tower catch on Saturday. If successful, it would mark the first time a spacecraft has returned from orbit to land vertically at a launch tower. The Bakersfield Californian reports: The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars. Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising. "Well, that certainly isn't the news that we had hoped to hear for today," observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong. This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) -- the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket -- an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.
The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight's end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket's self-destruct system was activated. The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages. You can watch a recorded livestream of the launch on YouTube.

item.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident.
In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information.
The outage also dealt a significant blow to independent sellers who rely on BrickLink for income. Simon Webster, who operates stores on both BrickLink and rival marketplace Brick Owl, reported that his overall sales revenue fell 52% over a four-day period, even as sales through Brick Owl rose 79%. "Their comms are amateur at the best of times, but surely they should be able to send an email to let sellers and buyers alike know what is happening and what they're doing to rectify it," Webster said. "But no, we're all left in the dark."
The incident has renewed concerns about BrickLink's aging infrastructure. Founded in 2000 and acquired by LEGO in 2019, the marketplace reportedly runs on a complex collection of interconnected systems that makes modernization difficult. The Brick Fanatics report questions whether the 25-year-old platform remains fit for purpose and whether prolonged outages and security concerns could push sellers toward competing marketplaces like Brick Owl.

item.title: RevOps Is Quietly Becoming an Engineering Job
item.author: Malek Damiri
item.content:encoded: Over the last two weeks, I've written here about a calendar table that knows November 1 has 25 hours, a customer health score that barely beats a coin flip, a 1961 warehouse formula that finds dead deals in a CRM, a Slack report that checks its own numbers before it posts, an exam for AI agents, a macOS job that died because of where it kept its log file, and why 3x pipeline coverage is a guess.My title is Head of Revenue Operations. Very little of that shows up in a RevOps job description.I started in supply chain, moved into revenue operations, and taught myself SQL along the way. For most of that time, the job looked the way people describe it: own the CRM, build the reports, run the forecast, keep sales and finance looking at the same numbers. That's still the job. But the way it gets done has changed, and I think it's changing faster than the job descriptions.The data moved into the warehouse. RevOps used to live inside the CRM and its report builder. Now the numbers that matter, from billing, product usage, payments, and the CRM itself, land in Snowflake or BigQuery. The person who reconciles them needs SQL, not a report wizard. An AI coding agent will write the script that syncs the CRM, builds the workbook, or posts the report in minutes. That's the real shift. When code is cheap, more of RevOps becomes code, and someone has to run it.Running it is the part that didn't get cheaper. A script is easy. A script that runs at 7:45 every morning for two years, survives a laptop update, posts nothing when the data is wrong, and tells someone when it didn't run at all: that's operations engineering. And it's increasingly a RevOps problem, because the scripts are about revenue and nobody else owns them.If you work in RevOps, sales ops, or finance ops and you're wondering where to invest, here's my list, roughly in order of how often each one has saved me. Not just SELECT and GROUP BY. Grain, joins that duplicate rows, window functions, time zones. Most wrong numbers I've chased came down to a join or a day boundary. (These six Snowflake patterns cover the ones I reach for every week.)One scheduler, and how it fails. cron, launchd, GitHub Actions, Airflow. Pick the one you'll actually use and learn what it does when things go wrong. Every scheduler has a way to fail silently. Know yours.Version control for anything that produces a number. If it ends up in front of a CFO, it goes in git. "Which version of the query made that slide?" should have an answer.Testing numbers, not just code. Reconciliations, check cells, golden questions with known answers. Code that runs is not code that's right. Somewhere to break things that isn't production, and a deliberate step between the two.Writing definitions down. Every metric needs a written definition that sales and finance have both agreed to. It's the least technical item on this list, and the one that prevents the most arguments. Give them a sandbox, an exam, and a short list of things they're never allowed to touch. Then let them do a lot of the typing.The risk in all of this is that RevOps turns into a shadow data engineering team: pipelines nobody else understands, a dozen scheduled jobs on one laptop, and a single person who knows how any of it works. That version is worse than not automating at all.So draw a line. Data engineering owns the platform: ingestion, the warehouse, the infrastructure everyone shares. RevOps owns the business logic and the last mile: the definitions, the reconciliations, the reports, and the small automations that move revenue numbers to the people who use them.And give the last mile an exit. When a RevOps automation becomes important enough that its failure would hurt the company, it graduates to the platform, with real monitoring, an owner on call, and a second person who understands it.The job description hasn't caught up.Most RevOps postings still ask for CRM administration, reporting, and strong analytical skills. Those matter. But the people I see doing this job well now are also comfortable in a terminal, can read a stack trace without panic, and treat a scheduled job like a product with users.The title still says operations. More and more, the work says engineering. The people who do well will be the ones who take both words seriously.I'm Malek Damiri, head of revenue operations in Atlanta. I write about revenue operations and the systems behind it at malekdamiri.com.

item.title: I Put a 42-Desk Design Studio Inside My Coding Agent
item.author: Aditya Reddy
item.content:encoded:
The part after the first design.In October, I pointed Desk Studio at its own launch card. Three roughs, one pick, three polish rounds, scored 8.4, then 8.5, then 8.9, signed off at 8.9 for $1.34 at list price. And I could see every one of those steps while it happened, which is the whole reason the tool exists.Before it, a follow-up like "make the headline bigger" would come back from my coding agent as a whole new design. New layout, new colors, sometimes new copy. Was the headline fixed? Couldn't tell, cause everything else moved too.So Desk Studio splits the job up like a small studio. Rough options first, then one gets picked with notes, a cheaper desk polishes it, a script checks the real pixels, and a senior desk signs it off or sends it back. I still use it on my own projects.There are 42 desks. The Design Manager runs in your own session and hands out work. The other 41 run as subagents, things like a Typographer, an Art Director, a UI Designer, or an Email Designer. Each one is just a markdown brief in the repo, so if you want to know how the Art Director decides, you open and read it.They're grouped into three tiers, and each tier is on a model that suits what it does.the pick, the notes, the sign-offthe roughs, research, type, tokens, copyevery polish round, the makingIt all runs locally. The desks reach models through whatever CLI you're already logged into, , or , or an API key if you'd rather. Apart from those model calls and a few web lookups from the research desks, nothing leaves your machine.In Claude Code it's a plugin. For Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf or OpenCode it's one line in the project:# Claude Code /plugin install desk --marketplace adityareddy-dev/deskstudio
# Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf, OpenCode npx deskstudio add Then you just ask like you normally would:/desk:design a launch card for LinkedIn
# or run the job yourself from a terminal npx --package deskstudio desk-run design "a launch card for LinkedIn" The files land in with a short note on who did what, the scores and the cost.Every visual job takes the same path. The UI Designer makes three different directions on the senior model, from the brief, your brand file and the standard for that kind of piece. The Art Director looks at the renders, picks one (or mixes two) and writes notes. A builder desk works from those notes plus a screenshot of the current render. Rounds are cheap, so this is where the back and forth happens. A script renders the file in Chrome at every size and checks the pixels. No model. The Creative Director scores eight axes: hierarchy, typography, spacing, colour, composition, originality, brand fit and copy.To pass, every axis needs 8 or more and the average needs 8.5. Fail-proof, and it goes back to the builder with the screenshot. A builder that misses the same note twice hands the file up to a senior, and a senior that misses twice gets one round with the Art Director. After the round cap, the job comes back marked under the bar, with a note on which axis fell short, so it won't quietly ship something that didn't pass.Here's a real terminal run of exactly that, on OpenAI models this time. Proof caught a type-scale problem in round 2, the builder fixed it, and round 3 still came back under the bar cause originality only got a 6. The last lines say what's missing.Splitting out the pick was deliberate. Once a direction is picked, every round after that is a fix to that one design, so a note like "type sizes, not layout" means the next round touches type sizes and nothing else. When every round is a fresh design, there's nothing steady to measure against, which was the whole problem in the first place.Proof has no model in it for a similar reason. Contrast against the real pixels, text spilling out of a box, a headline sitting in a platform's crop zone, a script checks all that the same way every time and it costs nothing. The models get to spend their judgment on the stuff a script can't see.One real job, start to finish.This is the launch card for Desk Studio itself, retold from its job record.The UI Designer made three roughs: an editorial split, a type-only one, and a framed one. The Art Director went with rough 2, the type-only one, and wrote why: "headline reads first at both sizes, only amber is the small lamp, fixes are type sizes not layout."You can overrule that. Every rough has a button, and if you use it, the pick goes on record as yours instead of the Art Director's.After that, the builder polished, proof ran every round, and the Creative Director scored each one.under the 8.5 bar, back to polishoriginality 7, under the bar, back to polishRound 3 got a 9 on seven axes and an 8 on originality, so 8.9 on average. This is the file it signed off.The whole job came to $1.34 at list price.the pick and three sign-offsAbout 60% of that went to judgment and 40% to making, and the three polish rounds together were ten cents. That's what the tiers are for. If you're on a subscription, it's a list-price estimate of usage, not an extra bill.The proof step, up close.Before the Creative Director ever sees a file, proof renders it in Chrome at each target size and checks:text contrast against the actual pixels behind itcolours inside the brand palette and type on the brand scalethat every required line of copy is actually therecarousel slides matching each other, and reading time and flashes in motion piecesYou can also run proof on its own against any HTML file:desk-proof check hero.html --brand .desk/DESIGN.md --sizes phone,desktop Watching it on the dashboard.1.1 rebuilt the dashboard into the floor you can leave open while a job runs. It only listens on , and the URL carries a token.# Claude Code /desk:dashboard setup /desk:dashboard start
# any other agent or a plain terminal npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard setup npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard start The strip at the top is the job. In this capture of the launch card, it's sitting on round 2's sign-off; round 1 came in at 8.4, $0.77 is spent so far, and it's 17m 25s in. holds the job before the next step, and ends it there. Neither one cuts a desk off halfway.Below that is the floor, with a room per tier and a Proof booth. Each desk is a little bot that wakes up while that desk is working and goes back to sleep after. A ×3 on a desk means three of them are running at once, which is what you see during the roughs. Every room's sign shows its model, and swaps the whole tier.Clicking a desk opens its panel. The UI Designer's panel here says it's on and has done 4 runs on this job, 887k tokens, $0.45. You can switch just that desk to another model, for this job or as the default, or leave it a note that goes into its next prompt.On the right is who's working right now, and under it the studio log in plain words. One line from this job reads "Creative Director scored round 1: 8.4, under the bar", and the polish for round 2 starts on the very next line.The roles and cost panel is where the tiers make sense. The builders went through 2.9 million tokens on this job, and that still came to ten cents. The slowest single run was the Creative Director's round 2 sign-off at 11 minutes 25 seconds, which tells you where the time actually goes.Since 1.0.2, a job's event log also exports as an OpenTelemetry trace, with role timings, tokens and cost, so a design job can sit in the same tracing tool as the rest of your stuff.The repo keeps a gallery of 17 signed-off pieces with their renders, scores and costs. Most are for four made-up brands, one's for a real site whose brand the studio found in the project, and three are for Desk Studio itself.Ops dashboard for NorthlightPitch deck for NorthlightThe scores come from the studio's own model reviewers. They're useful for comparing rounds of one job, not as a benchmark against anything else. The standalone runner only takes for social cards right now, and the rest of the commands are Claude Code skills. The briefs install into other agents fine, though not every command works the same way there yet.Free, MIT licensed, and it runs on the CLI login or API key you already have.npx deskstudio add npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard setup npx --package deskstudio desk-dashboard start Then ask your agent for a launch card and keep the floor open. The code, docs, and full gallery are on GitHub, and there's a 50-second film on deskstudio.ai.What I use most is the rounds view. I pull up round 1 next to round 3 and check if the thing I asked for is the thing that changed.

item.title: US Seizes $1.2 Billion In Crypto Stolen From Binance
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
U.S. authorities have seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen during Binance's $6 billion October hack, which the FBI attributes to North Korean military-linked hackers known as "TraderTraitor." The DOJ also said it disrupted infrastructure behind the "FaceStealer" deepfake scam, blamed for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency. CNBC reports: Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen. [...] The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency." That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said. DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets. But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.
Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said. The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts -- sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.

The Register reports: Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. item.title: Microsoft's Global Outage May Be Worse Than Amazon's Or Crowdstrike's, Expert Says
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: A global outage taking down a wide range of Microsoft 365 services remains ongoing Friday morning. The outage started midday Thursday, impacting users of Microsoft email, cloud, and AI services. Microsoft has documented the full list of services impacted by the error, while moving early Friday morning to protect customers around the world from losing emails during the extended disruptions. "Recovery actions are ongoing," the Microsoft 365 Status account confirmed on X. "To help preserve delayed mail during this event, we've extended email timeout to 48 hours."
Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like "one of the biggest outages of all time," Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even "worse," he suggested.
Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC's report documented various harms, noting that "few public bodies were immune from the outage." In some cases, doctors couldn't send patients "important" updates on medication changes or follow-up care. The financial sector suffered, too, with people blocked from making bank transfers since they couldn't receive verification codes.
Justice systems were also hobbled. The Supreme Court in the Philippines saw its legal work derailed, NBC reported. And one US sheriff's office in Colorado reported that the outage made it difficult for people to post bond for prisoners' immediate release. It's unclear how many users were affected, but Microsoft estimated in January that the total number of paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions exceeded 450 million. Microsoft's most recent updates confirmed that it's seeing "broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific."
"Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure," Microsoft said. "Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods."

item.title: Comparing Six AI Video APIs by Cost, Concurrency, and Reliability
item.author: Nica Furs
item.content:encoded: Most AI video work still starts in a browser tab: type a prompt, wait, download. That breaks down once a team needs 200 product clips a week, a video step inside an app, or an agent that renders drafts overnight. Video APIs move generation into code. In this article, we: how the requests work, a short working example, what matters once real traffic arrives, six APIs side by side, and the automation layer on top.How API Video Generation WorksA video takes anywhere from under a minute to a few minutes to render, so no provider keeps an HTTP connection open until the file is ready. Every major video API follows the same three-part pattern. You send a POST request with the model, prompt, and settings. The API answers right away with a request ID and a status URL. You poll the status URL, or register a webhook and wait. The job moves from queued to in progress, then to a terminal state such as completed or failed. The completed response holds a URL to the MP4. Download it to your own storage, because providers delete outputs: Replicate after one hour by default, Higgsfield after at least seven days.The names change from provider to provider. fal calls them requests, Replicate calls them predictions, and Runway calls them tasks. The shape stays the same.Step-by-Step Example: A Text-to-Video Request in PythonThe example below uses the Higgsfield API and Seedance 2.5. The same submit, poll, and download loop works with any provider. Only the URL, auth header, and field names change.Step 1: Set your credentials. Create an API key in the console and export the key ID and secret.export HF_API_KEY_ID="your-key-id" export HF_API_KEY_SECRET="your-key-secret" The idempotency key lets you resend the same request after a timeout without paying twice.import os, time, uuid, requestsAUTH = {"Authorization": f"Key {os.environ['HF_API_KEY_ID']}:{os.environ['HF_API_KEY_SECRET']}"} job = requests.post( "https://api.higgsfield.ai/bytedance/seedance-2.5/text-to-video", headers={**AUTH, "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())}, json={ "prompt": "A cinematic tracking shot along a sunlit coastal road", "resolution": "720p", "duration": 5, "aspect_ratio": "16:9", "generate_audio": True, }, timeout=30, ).json() print(job["request_id"], job["status"]) # -> queued Step 3: Poll until the job ends. Four statuses are terminal: completed, failed, nsfw, and canceled. TERMINAL = {"completed", "failed", "nsfw", "canceled"} while True: result = requests.get(job["status_url"], headers=AUTH, timeout=30).json() if result["status"] in TERMINAL: break time.sleep(5) Step 4: Download the video. if result["status"] == "completed": clip = requests.get(result["video"]["url"], timeout=120) with open("clip.mp4", "wb") as f: f.write(clip.content) else: print("Job ended with status:", result["status"], result.get("error")) The official Python SDK (pip install higgsfield-client) wraps steps 2 and 3 into a single subscribe() call. In production, replace the polling loop with a webhook: add an hf_webhook query parameter with your URL-encoded HTTPS endpoint, and Higgsfield sends a POST when the job reaches completed, failed, or nsfw.What Matters in Production WorkflowsA demo needs one successful call. A production pipeline has to survive timeouts, rate limits, moderation rejections, and bills that grow with every retry. Four areas decide how much work that takes.Every provider caps parallel jobs. Higgsfield allows 20 concurrent requests, fal allows 2 to 40 on self-serve accounts, Runway allows 1 to 20 depending on usage tier, and MiniMax allows 30 in-flight H3 jobs. Put your own job queue in front of the API, such as a database table or a Redis list, so a batch of 500 renders waits its turn instead of failing.Retry network errors and 5xx responses with exponential backoff. Never retry 4xx validation errors, since the same input will fail again. Send an idempotency key with each submission so a resent POST does not start a second paid job. Treat webhooks as at-least-once: Higgsfield, fal, and Replicate can all deliver duplicates, so deduplicate by request ID. Keep a polling fallback in case a webhook never arrives.Billing on Failed GenerationsFailure rules differ more than prices do. failed, timed-out, and NSFW-rejected requests are refunded automatically. 5xx server errors are free; 422 invalid-input errors can still be charged if a GPU already worked on the request. failed runs on public models are free; canceled runs on official models may be billed. credits come back when an error on Runway's side fails a job, but input moderation rejections are not refunded.Validate inputs before you submit. A broken image URL or an unsupported duration is the cheapest bug to catch.No single model wins every shot. Kling 4.0 handles long takes, Seedance 2.5 handles reference-driven scenes, and MiniMax H3 delivers 2K at a low rate. Calling each vendor directly means separate keys, balances, rate limits, and response formats. Platforms such as Higgsfield, fal, Replicate, and Runway Dev put multiple models behind one key and one balance, so switching models means changing one model ID. The trade-off is dependence on the platform’s pricing and model coverage.Prices are list rates per second of 720p video (768p on MiniMax), checked in late October and early November 2026. Promotions are excluded.50+ video and image models, incl. Kling 4.0, Seedance 2.5, MiniMax H3, Wan 3.0Wan 3.0 from $0.020/s; Kling 4.0 from $0.110/sLarge third-party catalogKling 3.0 Standard $0.084/sWebhook, polling, or status streamOfficial, community, and custom modelsNot billed on public modelsGen-4.5 and Aleph, plus Kling 4.0, Seedance 2.5, Gemini OmniRefunded on Runway-side errorsSync call or background modeGoogle shut down the three Veo 3.1 preview models in the Gemini API (veo-3.1-generate-preview, veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview, and veo-3.1-lite-generate-preview) on October 22, 2026, and points developers to Gemini Omni Flash instead. The generally available Veo 3.1 models remain on Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.Pick Higgsfield when you want top models plus production tools like consistent characters and camera control behind one key, or fal for a broad open catalog. Replicate fits teams that also deploy custom models. Runway Dev makes sense when Gen-4.5 and Aleph editing sit at the center of the pipeline. The Gemini API suits chat-style edits on Google's own model, and MiniMax wins when 2K output at a low per-second rate matters most.Automating Video GenerationA cron job or a cloud scheduler, such as GitHub Actions, Google Cloud Scheduler, or AWS EventBridge, can read tomorrow's briefs from a sheet or database, submit one job per row, and write the finished URLs back. Pair it with webhooks so the scheduler never sits idle polling.Both connect to any video API through a generic HTTP step, with no custom node required. In n8n, a typical flow runs Schedule Trigger, then HTTP Request to submit, then a Wait node set to resume on a webhook call, then a download and upload to Google Drive or S3. Pass $execution.resumeUrl as the provider's webhook URL so the workflow wakes up when the video is ready. In Make, one scheduled scenario submits jobs through the HTTP module, and a second scenario that starts from a Custom webhook receives results and files them.The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an AI assistant call outside tools directly. Higgsfield's MCP server connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, and other MCP-compatible clients, and gives the agent 30+ image and video models with no API key. A marketer can ask the assistant to make three 9:16 hook variants of a product shot and get the files back without writing code. Agents work best on drafts and one-off requests. Scheduled pipelines still handle volume better.Which AI video API is the cheapest? Per second of output, Wan 3.0 on Higgsfield starts at $0.020, MiniMax H3 runs $0.08 at 768p, and Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash costs about $0.10 at 720p. Count retries too: a cheap model that needs four takes costs more than a pricier one that lands in one.Do I need webhooks, or is polling enough? Polling every 5 to 10 seconds works at low volume. As job counts grow, webhooks cut wasted requests. Keep polling as a fallback either way.How long do providers keep generated videos? Not long. Replicate deletes API outputs after one hour by default, and Higgsfield keeps them at least seven days. Copy each file to your own storage as soon as the job completes.Can I spend web app credits through the API? Usually not. Higgsfield and Runway both bill API usage from a separate prepaid balance, apart from app subscriptions.

item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang's return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED. An internal "suggestion box" post submitted before Huang's resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company's board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
"If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," wrote one anonymous commenter. "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance," wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang's exit. "I stand by Jensen," the staffer wrote. "Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us."
[...] It's been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang's resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn't identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn't authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang's reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," the employee tells WIRED.
Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment "about Jensen's continuing as our CEO." Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. "If America fails the man who helped build its future," the employee in the companywide email stated, "then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang."

item.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.Turning a Windows defense against itselfThe attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

item.title: Building a Multi-Agent Website Launch Validator With OpenMinion
item.author: Alan De Bortolo
item.content:encoded:
I run a small web agency. We build and host websites for small businesses in the US and Brazil, and every launch has the same floor: a title and a description, a canonical URL, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, icons, a sitemap, a 404 page that really returns 404, an , and a that does not lock AI search crawlers out. For years we checked that list by hand, one tab per item.For Cortensor Hackathon 5, I turned the checklist into an agent called , built on OpenMinion 0.1, the agent SDK from the Cortensor ecosystem. It answers one question: is this site ready, ready with warnings, or blocked? The code is MIT-licensed at github.com/DesignMaster-Solutions/golive-gate and there is a 2-minute demo at youtu.be/tVH-x62QV3I.This post is about the one design decision that made it trustworthy, and about what it looks like to run an agent on open, swappable inference instead of one vendor's API.The rule: the model never fetches anythingThe tempting version of this agent is one prompt: "here is a URL, tell me if it is ready". That version hallucinates. It will tell you a sitemap exists because sites usually have one.So Go-Live Gate is split in three agents with different powers: It can call three read-only tools: , and . They are plain with 15-second timeouts and they return facts only (title length, which Open Graph tags exist, which bots blocks, the HTTP status of a random missing path). If the model skips a tool, the gap is filled deterministically, so the next step never guesses. It gets the raw facts and must return a pydantic-validated : a verdict plus one row per check with the evidence and the fix. The judge has no tools at all. It cannot fetch, so it cannot invent. A third agent must call , a tool marked . OpenMinion routes that call through a human approval callback (an interactive y/N, or for CI). If the human says no, nothing is written.Every run writes next to . A reviewer can open both and check the model's verdict against what the tools actually saw. That file is the whole point: the agent is only as honest as the layer under it, and that layer has its own offline tests against a local HTTP server.class Check(BaseModel): name: str status: Literal["pass", "warn", "fail"] evidence: str # the fact from a tool result that justifies the status fix: str = ""
class GoLiveReport(BaseModel): site: str verdict: Literal["ready", "ready_with_warnings", "blocked"] checks: list[Check] summary: str Why this matters for decentralized inferenceWhen the facts live in code and the model only reasons over them, the model becomes replaceable. That is what makes open inference practical for a business tool.OpenMinion talks to any OpenAI-compatible provider. Our recorded runs used a free open-weight model (nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free through OpenRouter); the same project is set up for the Cortensor Portal with one command (setup --provider cortensor-portal). I did not have to rewrite prompts or tools to switch. The judge's output is validated by a schema either way, so a weaker or slower node fails loudly instead of quietly writing a wrong verdict.If you are building on a decentralized inference network, you cannot assume the same model, the same latency or the same token limits on every call. Designing the agent so that the model is the least trusted part is how you get repeatable results anyway.The hackathon asked for building blocks tested and lessons learned, and these were the useful ones:Read-only tools still asked for confirmation. A tool tagged and still came back as "Policy confirmation required ... reply yes", because the decorator default wins over the tags. Declaring fixed it.The first request of every turn was not my agent. It was the automatic memory extractor, carrying the whole system prompt but exposing only one tool, . A model replaying that request alone said "the inspection tools are not available", and I spent an hour thinking my tools were hidden. A top-level "brain": {"auto_fact_extraction": {"enabled": false}} in removes that round trip.One turn did not fit a free tier. With default tools, the main turn sent about 17k characters of system prompt plus eight built-in tools. Groq answered at 8,683 tokens. Free tiers also need pacing the SDK does not have (its retry waits 300 ms; the rate window is 60 s), so I wrapped the adapter to stay under 6.5k tokens per minute. is not enforced on the model. The judge once answered with a markdown table. A JSON schema at the end of the instructions changed nothing; the same schema inside the user message worked on the first try. in the same session lost the first message, so retries now resend the facts.And one bug was mine. The first live run flagged a 697-character title on a client site whose real title is 63 characters. My parser was concatenating the elements inside inline SVG icons. The agent repeated what the tool reported, which is exactly why the facts layer has regression tests and the model does not get the last word.On capegraniteconnection.com, a site we built, the gate returned with 11 checks: title 63 characters, description 149, canonical present, all four Open Graph tags, 12 JSON-LD types including LocalBusiness and FAQPage, , both icons, no AI crawler blocked, a sitemap with 44 URLs, a 3,902-byte , and a real 404. On a free model the investigator took 232 seconds and the judge 355. Slow, but it runs unattended before every launch, and it is cheaper than the hour of tabs it replaces.python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python -m unittest test_checks -v .venv/bin/python gate.py yoursite.com --auto-approve yes The lesson I would carry to any agent on open infrastructure: let code collect the facts, let the model reason over them, put a schema on the answer and a human in front of anything that writes. Then the model can come from anywhere.

item.title: AARO Solved Iraq's 'Jellyfish' as Balloons. Alaska's Jellyfish UFO Still Lacks the Data
item.author: Anomaly Detection
item.content:encoded: A June sighting in Anchorage went viral in November. Two witnesses, one camera, a rainbow, a military base somewhere behind the treeline, and far more questions than verified answers.A Rainbow, a Treeline and an Object With TentaclesAt about 10:13 p.m. Alaska Daylight Time on June 15, 2026, Sara Jane Osborn was photographing a rainbow from a car on Sixth Avenue in Anchorage when she noticed a dark, black-and-silver shape above the trees. Her husband, Pete, pulled into an empty downtown parking lot so she could shoot unobstructed. Osborn described dangling appendages that seemed to move independently as the shape turned side to side, and said it was visible for roughly three minutes before it "disappeared almost as quickly as it came," according to IBTimes UK, which drew on a November 10 Daily Mail interview.The couple then searched a nearby park for a kite flyer and drove toward Arctic Valley, looking for about 30 minutes without finding an operator or another witness. That fruitless search is part of their testimony. It is not proof that a kite was impossible. Asked who knows what she saw, Osborn offered: "Only God and the government." She also allowed, "maybe it's a drone-type thing."Two eyewitnesses are named: Sara Jane and Pete Osborn. Only Sara Jane is credited as the camera operator. Coverage that says the couple "captured" the object does not establish two independently operated cameras.The defensible public count as of November 12: one witness, one phone, several still photos taken in quick succession, followed by one video, per IBTimes UK. No outlet we reviewed published the video's length or the total number of stills. The clips circulating on X and Instagram, including an X post by Mario Nawfal and a screengrab WION credits to X user @digijordan, appear to be reposts, crops or excerpts of the same encounter. Counting reposts as independent sightings would be misleading.No verified second-angle recording was located. Nor was an original uncompressed file, complete EXIF metadata, camera specifications, verified geolocation or an authenticated radar track. WION says plainly that it "cannot independently verify the authenticity" of the footage. five months between capture and publication is a long time for a file to travel through messaging apps and social platforms, each of which strips metadata and recompresses video. Provenance standards like C2PA can, in principle, ride along with a file, but provenance metadata is only useful if it survives, and as Paul Krause argues on HackerNoon, records attached to a file can simply be stripped. The single most valuable artifact in this story is still the original file on Osborn's phone.Was It Over Military Land? The Map MattersThe couple believed the object sat toward Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson (JBER). Pete estimated it was within about three miles. IBTimes UK notes that neither the distance nor any link to the base or military airspace has been verified. An object visually aligned with military land may be much closer to the camera. Without a reliable range, azimuth and camera position, no one can say whether it entered restricted airspace.The published still adds a useful constraint. In the frame, the object hangs in front of a sunlit, forested mountainside, not against open sky (see the feature image). Whatever it was, it was nearer to the camera than that slope. That fits a modest-range object at least as well as a giant distant one.The Sun Was Up, and Behind Them"10:13 p.m." sounds like night. In Anchorage in mid-June, it isn't. Sunset that week falls around 11:39 p.m. at an azimuth of about 328 degrees, and civil twilight runs all night. Using the standard NOAA solar-position approximation, we estimate the sun sat roughly 6 degrees above the horizon in the northwest at the time of the sighting.Two things follow. First, a rainbow always forms opposite the sun, so Osborn was facing generally east to southeast, toward the Chugach front range, which is consistent with a sightline toward the eastern reaches of JBER and Arctic Valley. Second, a low sun behind the camera front-lights everything in view. That helps explain a "silver" sheen on a dark object. Reflective fabric, foil or Mylar would flash brightly in exactly that light.It also rules out one famous lookalike. A "space jellyfish" is a rocket exhaust plume lit by the sun high above a ground observer who is in twilight darkness. Osborn was standing in daylight, and the object was in front of a mountainside, not 100 miles up.Does It Really Look Like a Jellyfish?Visually, yes, at a descriptive level. A domed upper mass with thin dangling projections evokes a jellyfish drifting through water, and the resemblance strengthens when the appendages flex and the body rotates. But resemblance is not taxonomy. Helium decorations, show kites, balloon bundles, fabric, debris and compression artifacts can all produce organic silhouettes.Real jellyfish move by contracting a bell to push water. The Anchorage object has not been shown to pulse in a matching locomotion cycle, and the available clips do not establish its speed, altitude or any controlled acceleration. "It looked alive" is a witness impression, not a biological or aerospace finding.The Best Ordinary Explanations, and What Each Would Need to Prove Long fabric streamers and wind-driven rotation fit the silhouette. Inflatable octopus and jellyfish show kites are commercial products, sold in sizes like an 8-meter octopus. A visible tether, an identified operator or a weather-consistent trajectory would strengthen the case. Note that under the FAA's Part 101 rules, kites flown high or near an airport require notice to air traffic control, and Anchorage has several airports, including JBER and Merrill Field. The couple's failure to find a flyer does not eliminate the explanation, and Osborn's own reasoning ("why would you only fly it for, like, three minutes?") is a fair question rather than evidence.Balloon cluster or novelty balloon. A buoyant object can drift and rotate while ribbons swing on their own. Close-ups showing seams or strings, or a reconstruction against wind data, would test it. This is the explanation that resolved the most famous previous "jellyfish" (see below). Mechanically possible, but there is no evidence of a drone, operator, motor noise or flight record. Since March 2024, the FAA has fully enforced its Remote ID rule, which requires most drones to broadcast identification and location. A compliant drone would have been detectable by any nearby receiver at the time; no one has reported such a capture.Digital manipulation or AI generation. Possible in principle, but no forensic analysis of the original file has been published either way. As HackerNoon contributor Matthew of Technology News Australia observes, despite ubiquitous cameras no one has produced one clear, independently verified photograph of an alien craft. Blurry phone footage keeps both the believers' and skeptics' cases unfalsifiable.Perspective and apparent size. The couple recalled an aircraft that looked much smaller than the object. That comparison cannot establish size unless both distances are known. The Pentagon's AARO paper on forced perspective and parallax explains why apparently huge or fast objects routinely mislead observers.As of November 12, no aerospace engineer, meteorologist, imaging-forensics specialist or AARO investigator has publicly authenticated or solved this recording. Claims of expert confirmation should be treated with caution. IBTimes UK states explicitly that the object's identity, location and link to the base remain unverified.The base rate is worth knowing. AARO's FY2025 annual report, summarized by New Space Economy, counted 319 new reports. Of the 114 incoming cases it closed, 60 were balloons and 44 were satellites. The Pentagon's 2024 historical UAP review found no verified evidence of extraterrestrial technology and noted that many unresolved cases simply lack adequate data. Neither is a determination about this video.Al Taqaddum Air Base, Iraq, October 23, 2017. The infrared "jellyfish UAP" that Jeremy Corbell released in January 2024 was filmed from a force-protection aerostat over the base. In September 2025, AARO assessed with high confidence that it was a cluster of fully and partially inflated balloons drifting with the wind at roughly 4 to 14 mph and 850 to 2,200 feet, with no heat signature from motors. It is a separate case with a different sensor and does not corroborate Anchorage, but it is the closest precedent: dangling strings, apparent shape-shifting and a military backdrop, all resolved as balloons once the full footage and geometry were analyzed. The Metabunk forum thread documents how independent analysts reached the same answer.Stroud area, England, February 10, 1989. Drivers near the A46 reported a jellyfish-like aerial object, according to a recap citing the Swindon Star's front page. The account rests on old newspaper reports, with no comparable imagery.Fresno area, California, April 2023. A tentacled object drew comparisons to sci-fi creatures until zoomed footage showed strings consistent with a novelty kite, per the same recap. A useful cautionary counterexample, not a debunking of Anchorage.What Could Actually Settle the Alaska StoryThe useful next steps are concrete: obtain Osborn's original phone files and full photo burst; check capture timestamps and GPS metadata; pin down the exact Sixth Avenue and parking-lot positions; reconstruct the rainbow and mountain sightlines (the solar geometry above is a start); identify the lens focal length; pull wind profiles at several altitudes; check FAA records, Part 101 kite notices and any Remote ID logs; request a JBER public-affairs response; and look for other cameras pointed east that evening.The open question is not whether the silhouette is strange. It is. The questions are whether the object was near or far, how it moved relative to the wind, whether its disappearance was real acceleration or just loss of visibility, and whether anyone else filmed it. Until those are answered, the most precise description is "an unidentified object in one witness's video," not an alien vehicle over a military base.The Anchorage jellyfish is real as a reported encounter: a named woman and her husband say they saw something unusual, and her imagery surfaced five months later. The viral claims, including giant size, flight directly over JBER, impossible motion, multiple independent films and extraterrestrial origin, remain unverified. The one still in public view places the object in daylight, front-lit by a low sun, in front of a mountainside. The last famous jellyfish turned out to be balloons. This one deserves the same patient analysis, starting with the original file.

The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports: The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.
[...] Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system's coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News. The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

item.title: Packaging Innovation for Good
item.author: Brian Wallace
item.content:encoded: The European Union has declared an ultimatum against unsustainability: all consumer packaging placed on the EU market must be designed for recycling by 2030. This mandate was announced by the and formally became law in all 27 EU member states on Aug. 12, 2026. Since then, the mandate has placed restrictions on synthetic “forever chemicals” (PFAS) in food packaging as part of the “Design for Recycling” (DfR) framework, which will become the baseline by 2030. It is significantly reshaping how companies design, import and sell products globally.All packaged products must meet these regulatory changes, not just those manufactured in the EU. Because many brands prefer to standardize packaging across different nations’ markets, it is probable that PPWR’s influence will reach well beyond Europe as brands change their designs to streamline operations.Under PPWR, materials will be graded based on their recyclability performance rates through the DfR framework. Grade A materials are __≥95% recyclable__and meet the highest circular life cycle standards. Grade B materials are ≥80% recyclable and are still considered to be highly efficient. Materials graded as C are ≥70% recyclable. Any material rated below 70% is deemed unrecyclable and will be banned from all markets.The new rules imply that paperboard is one of the best materials for long-term reuse, reducing and recycling because it combines a high recyclability rate and excellent compatibility with set content targets. This paper-based material can be recycled 5-10 times into innovative packaging for consumer retailers and their customers. After it is responsibly disposed of, the cycle starts again for this valuable material. European waste systems reportedly recover 87% of paper and paperboard packaging for reuse. This significantly outperforms plastic, which has just a . Other fiber-based materials help companies adjust to the tightening restrictions and mandates on single-use plastic packaging while simultaneously supporting enduring goals made for resource efficiency and overall recyclability.The first rising concern about single-use plastics began in the 2010s. By 2022, the European Commission proposed PPWR to replace the outdated Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (PPWD) of 1994. By February 2025, PPWR went into full effect. In the coming years, the development of secondary legislation will start. By 2028, mandatory standardized labels will appear on consumer packaging and on all waste sorting receptacles. Later on in the early 2030s, all packaging in the EU, whether locally produced or imported, will officially meet DfR criteria. Most plastic packaging and plastic parts will meet initial minimum recycled content requirements. By the end of the decade, all packaging must meet even stricter criteria for recyclability to ensure an even more sustainable world.The PPWR intends to set a binding packaging waste reduction target of . Brands that adapt to the DfR mandates from the start by adopting paperboard material and designing for a circular material lifecycle will be better prepared for decades to come. Additionally, they will also gain an advantage in a competitive market where environmental sustainability is rapidly becoming the criterion.

Organizations must also secure the data, infrastructure, and autonomous systems that increasingly power their operations.GITEX Cyber Valley will bring these conversations together through tailored business meetings and private briefings for global cybersecurity leaders, creating opportunities to examine how organizations can scale AI capabilities while protecting the systems and information they depend on.Global Cybersecurity Leaders Take the StageGITEX GLOBAL 2026 will feature an extensive lineup of cybersecurity companies showcasing technologies and solutions across the security ecosystem.Confirmed cybersecurity exhibitors include Acronis, AMIVIZ, Cohesity, Commvault, Forcepoint, Forescout, Kaspersky, ManageEngine, NETSCOUT, Netskope, NinjaOne, Proofpoint, SentinelOne / Sentinel Labs, and Trellix.Their participation reflects the breadth of the cybersecurity landscape, spanning data protection, endpoint security, network defense, threat detection, and enterprise resilience.The UAE Cybersecurity Council will also participate, alongside other government institutions and public-sector entities, highlighting the importance of collaboration between national cybersecurity strategies and private-sector innovation.Why AI Is Changing the Cybersecurity ConversationThe growing adoption of AI is creating new opportunities for businesses, but it is also expanding the attack surface.AI-powered applications, autonomous agents, cloud infrastructure, and connected systems introduce new security considerations. Organizations must account for how AI systems access information, interact with other applications, and operate within critical business environments. At the same time, the emergence of quantum computing is prompting organizations to consider the long-term resilience of their encryption and data protection strategies.These developments make AI security and post-quantum readiness increasingly important areas of discussion for cybersecurity professionals, technology providers, and government decision-makers.GITEX GLOBAL's wider focus on sovereign AI, frontier models, agentic AI, and sovereign security provides a broader context for these discussions, connecting cybersecurity with the infrastructure and technologies shaping the next phase of digital transformation.GITEX Global 2026: A Global Meeting Point for Technology and CybersecurityBeyond its cybersecurity programme, GITEX GLOBAL 2026 will bring together more than 6,000 global technology enterprises, government entities, and startups, alongside 1000+ investors representing nearly US$2 trillion in assets under management.The 2026 edition also introduces a new venue and format.
