item.title: Tech Adoption Is a Cultural Problem: Why UX Habits Beat Innovation
item.author: Daria Volkova
item.content:encoded: "You’re using our platform wrong."Oh no, sweetheart. Culture doesn’t adapt to your technology.Stop blaming Mercury in retrograde when users refuse to abandon their old habits for your shiny new tool. The pattern is always the same: the best tool in the room loses to the one people already trust. Founders file this failure under pricing, onboarding, or "users who need education." In reality, it belongs under culture.My name is I help tech companies explain what makes their products different and why they matter. At university, I studied sociology and cultural studies. It taught me to look at people in groups first, and products second.Look at the current wave of AI: the had stellar backers, deep pockets, and massive hype. It was dead in a year. was a plain text box, and it became the fastest-growing app in history. Same period, same underlying tech, and culture decided which one survived.In 2020, a Japanese minister went to war on two office objects: the fax machine and the hanko, the small personal seal people stamp in red ink instead of signing. (Minister for Digital Transformation of Japan) had the power and the better technology. A signed PDF is faster, cheaper, and easier to search than a stamped fax. He got most government offices to agree to drop the seal. Years later, the fax still hums and the seal still sits in the drawer.The seal survived because in Japan it was never only a tool. It stands for identity and consent. A company, a bank, and a neighbor all read it the same way. A better tool cannot push out a habit the whole country trusts.In , credit cards never caught on; by 2021 only about 38 percent of adults had one. So people skipped the card and went from cash straight to the QR code.Today two apps, , handle more than nine in ten mobile payments, from the fruit stall to the temple donation box.The same thing happens inside companies now. A team gets a powerful new AI tool, and people keep working the old way, because the old way is the one they trust.How did manage to become so popular and usher in a new era of consumer AI? People already knew how to type a question into a box, the way they type into Google or a chat with a friend.More than a million people tried it in five days. Around 100 million were using it two months after launch. TikTok took nine months to reach that number. Instagram took more than two years.ChatGPT did not ask us to adopt a new habit or buy a new device. The company didn't ruin our familiar flow.Strong tech can still read the room wrongThe launched in 2024 with huge attention. It clipped to your shirt, had no screen, and answered out loud or showed tiny text on your palm. To use it, people had to wear a new device, learn new hand gestures, and talk to their own chest in public.By the summer, the company was taking back more pins each day than it sold. In 2025, HP bought what was left for 116 million dollars and switched the pins off.The , another AI gadget from the same year, got the same cold response. Both asked people to build a habit from zero, with nothing pushing them to do it.Great tech can still misjudge the culture it lands in. In February 2024, added image generation to Asked for pictures of people from history, it often returned images that did not match the record. The reaction was loud and fast. Within days, Google paused the feature for images of people. The fix took months.Respect the culture, or build a bridgeThe temptation for founders and product builders is always to focus on the raw technology: the compute power, the model architecture, the sheer wizardry of what a tool can do. But history rewards the technology that integrates seamlessly into how humans already behave.If you are building something new, you have only two choices:Fit into existing culture and routines: Design your product around habits people already practice every single day. Meet them where they live: in the text box, the chat window, or their current workflow. If your technology requires people to act differently, you must make the transition so effortless and the value so overwhelming that they voluntarily unlearn the old way.Tech fails when it assumes people will change their culture just to use a clever tool. Culture is stubborn, patient, and deeply rooted. Ignore human behavior, and your brilliant creation will end up abandoned.💬 Have a story to share or want to add your example of tech product adoption? Let me know in the comments.

item.title: The Digital Euro: Solving Problems You Didn’t Have, With Rules You Don’t Write
item.author: Ras Vasilisin
item.content:encoded: Do you actually need a digital euro because payments weren’t convenient enough already?I pay for everything with my phone. Instantly. Even when I’m abroad. To be fair, I’m still glad we actually get to live in the 21st century.And no, it’s not because they want to ban cash. Cash is already quietly fading out of daily use in Europe. It’s certainly not because someone at a central bank suddenly developed a burning passion for transparency and democratisation.So let’s look at what’s actually being built, who gets to set the rules, and most importantly, why it’s being built at all.A pilot is not a public launch(It’s just the rehearsal where nobody gets to leave)According to ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone’s speech on 5 November 2026, they plan a 12-month pilot in the second half of 2027.It will involve 36 payment service providers, including Deutsche Bank, UniCredit, Revolut, Stripe, and Adyen. Testing will cover ordinary situations: purchases, transfers, and refunds.Harmless on paper. For now.2029 is more of a wish than a deadlineAccording to the ECB, the target for a possible first issuance is 2029, but only if the necessary legislation is adopted by the end of 2026. Only then would the Governing Council decide whether to issue it at all.Preparing a system and approving its use are two separate decisions. News headlines tend to treat them as the same thing.These aren’t “your” depositsIt might come as a shock, but the balance you see in your banking app isn’t actually your money. It’s a promise from your local bank that they’ll repay it one day. A digital euro would move that promise even further away, all the way behind the walls of the ECB headquarters in Frankfurt.Apart from that minor detail, your brand-new digital euro would be almost identical to what you already use.It would still be worth one euro. It would still appear on your screen as if you owned it. And it would still not be immune to money printing, inflation, or devaluation.Under the proposed design it wouldn’t even pay the princely 0.05% interest some accounts currently offer. And there would be a limit on how much you could hold. Roughly €3,000 was one of the options analysed, not a final rule.Europe doesn’t want to depend on Visa and MastercardNow, to be fair, there is one legitimate point in favor of the digital euro.For card payments, Europe still depends heavily on non-European companies, in practice, mainly Visa and Mastercard. A shared European payments infrastructure makes sense as a political and economic objective. The real test is whether regular people actually get enough out of the digital euro to bother switching.Good luck convincing 450 million people to just switch up their daily habits. Especially when the new system arrives with holding limits, no interest, and a few extra questions about why you’re using it.Now for the part everyone’s actually worried about: privacy.For offline payments, the intention is cash-like privacy, personal transaction details known only to the payer and the recipient.That does not mean the entire wallet would operate anonymously like cash. Anti-money-laundering checks would still apply when depositing, transferring or withdrawing funds.If losing privacy on offline transactions worries you, online payments are a whole different story. Naturally, the ECB promises to process data so it can’t be traced straight back to you. Your bank or payment provider would still have identification and other legal obligations.In other words, the ECB says it will not monitor everything you buy. Your local bank will.The ECB says the digital euro would not be programmable money. The issuer wouldn’t dictate where, when or on what you could spend it. That’s different from a conditional payment you choose to arrange yourself.So there’s no need for panic about your money expiring or a sudden ban on steak purchases.There is a good reason to check whether protection against such restrictions remains firmly written into the final rules. A press release is no substitute for a legal safeguard.The same applies to cash. The ECB says the digital euro would complement it, not replace it. What matters is whether people can actually keep using cash, and whether pulling it out of your wallet is still treated as normal rather than vaguely suspicious.The digital euro and Bitcoin serve different purposes.A digital euro would remain a euro, governed by monetary and public institutions.As I learned the hard way after a single copy-paste mistake sent a test transfer straight into oblivion: with Bitcoin, I don’t need a central issuer to hold or send my money. The catch? If I hold my own keys, protecting them is entirely on me.Bitcoin isn’t magically anonymous, either. Its public ledger and wild price swings don’t vanish just because we’re fed up with central banks.I judge the digital euro on whether it actually fixes payments without chipping away at our rights. I judge Bitcoin on its own merits and risks. They’re playing entirely different games.The digital euro isn’t about easier coffee purchases.Money is a form of expression. How we spend it, who we send it to, and whether we can do so with a degree of privacy is part of personal freedom. If we trade that for a new shiny digital euro, we may one day discover we have lost both the convenience and the freedoms.Once the rules are written and the system is live, complaining that “this wasn’t what we signed up for” will be largely irrelevant.The real question isn’t whether the digital euro happens.It’s whether we wake up in time to realize our right to use our own money is being quietly rewritten. Politely, step by step, and backed by world-class PR.

item.title: Educational Byte: What Is a Liquidity Pool in Crypto —and Why It Matters
item.author: Obyte
item.content:encoded: To understand this one, let’s first look at the "traditional" processes for exchanging money via digital platforms. We can commonly see two mechanisms: you exchange your currency directly against the exchange or provider’s own funds, or an order book is used. This order book records all buy and sell orders placed by users and provides liquidity based on that activity. The more orders in place, the more liquidity. Well, liquidity pools have come to replace these models in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) protocols.A liquidity pool in crypto is a supply of tokens locked inside a smart contract on a DeFi protocol. It has the purpose of offering liquidity to other users for swaps, loans, or any financial activity on that specific protocol. The locked funds come from other users who, in exchange for providing this liquidity to the pool, receive rewards in the form of transaction fees and even .This way, no powerful middlemen are required to safely access financial instruments. It’s the users themselves who provide liquidity in a decentralized environment.How Does a Liquidity Pool Work?Typically, a liquidity pool holds two tokens, such as GBYTE and USDC. Liquidity providers are the ones who deposit these token pairs—and they could be anyone with the available funds. Then, those funds help to create a big reserve that traders can use for their own operations, like swaps. The smart contract keeps track of those balances and applies the rules that govern each trade. comes from the reserves themselves. In a classic Automated Market Maker (AMM) model, a simple formula is used: X × Y = K, where X and Y represent the quantities of the two tokens and K is the constant. When someone swaps, let’s say, USDC for GBYTE, the pool receives one asset and releases the other, changing the balances and thus the price for the next trade. Depending on the available liquidity, a larger trade may create more price impact, which implies that the price could drop by a certain percentage for the next swap.For liquidity providers, the platform may give them LP tokens as proof of their share of the pool. These tokens can be used to track and redeem that share, including the depositor’s portion of trading fees earned by the pool. Their reward is directly proportional to their contribution to the pool.Some pools may be rewarded with additional incentives. For instance, in the Obyte-based DEX , all to a few selected pools receive 100 GBYTE every seven days, distributed in proportion to their contributed liquidity. That’s an additional incentive on top of fees.Why Does This Model Matter?A healthy financial environment needs liquidity, and liquidity doesn’t come out of nowhere. For trades and other operations to actually happen, funds must be available, and someone must put the funds there. In traditional finance, that someone is often a powerful middleman, like a bank. But cryptocurrencies weren’t created to rely on powerful middlemen; they were created to get rid of them. So, we have liquidity pools instead.By using this model, everyone can access liquidity without cumbersome requirements or censorship risks. Meanwhile, liquidity providers receive rewards for their contributions in what is, without a doubt, a type of investment that can yield a good and frequent passive return. Of course, the specific rules and the vary from network to network.uses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) structure without miners or “validators,” which increases its decentralization and drastically reduces the mere possibility of censorship or blocking. In Oswap.io, each pool has its own parameters and governance, but all are decentralized and open for everyone to participate. That’s the whole idea; that’s why liquidity pools matter: they offer a freedom we can’t enjoy in traditional financial products.Featured Vector Image by pikisuperstar /

item.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Exit Is a Wake-Up Call for Startup Founders
item.author: Bruce Li
item.content:encoded: The Unthinkable Happened on a ThursdayI had to read the headline three times.This morning, November 12, 2026, Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang had resigned as President, CEO, and director, . CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its , which tells you it had been a one-man show for 33 years.The board's word is "resigned." Most headlines went with "ousted." Days earlier, CBS had reported the board was to remove him. You decide which word fits.Here's the short version. A New York Times report alleged multiple affairs, including one with a Singapore data-center executive whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, at a firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia hardware. Another alleged affair was with a senior executive who reported directly to him. Huang had already admitted infidelity in a memo to employees on November 9. Then came national-security questions, demands from lawmakers, and a stock that fell roughly 10%, wiping out hundreds of billions in market value. After that, the end came quickly.Set the morality aside for a minute, because the board didn't need to settle it. What I want founders to notice is the .Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in a Denny's in 1993. He bet the company on GPUs, then on CUDA, then on AI, and grew it into a company worth more than $4 trillion. He is about as close to a founder-god as Silicon Valley has.And he had no structural protection whatsoever.Nvidia has a single class of stock: one share, one vote. Its board was made up of independent directors plus Jensen, and it could remove the CEO with or without cause by simple majority. Mark Zuckerberg can't be fired. Larry Page couldn't be fired. Jensen Huang, the man who made the AI age possible, could be shown the door in a week.If that doesn't make every founder reading this check their charter, nothing will.Why Founders Fall: A Short History of Losing Your Own CompanyFounders don't usually lose control in one dramatic boardroom scene. They lose it gradually, through a series of small and individually reasonable decisions.Act I: One share, one vote. For about sixty years the NYSE refused to list companies with dual-class shares. The idea was that voting power should track economic risk. Ford's 1956 IPO, where the family kept super-voting shares, was the famous exception. Media dynasties like the New York Times Company got a pass on the grounds of editorial independence.Act II: Google changes the rules. In 2004, Larry Page and Sergey Brin took Google public with Class B shares carrying . The public bought it anyway. Facebook, LinkedIn, Snap, and Alibaba all followed. Hong Kong held out, lost Alibaba's $25 billion IPO to New York, and changed its rules in 2018. By 2021–22, about were dual-class.Act III: the slow loss of your majority. This is the part nobody puts in the pitch deck. According to Carta's 2025–26 data, founders typically hold: after Series A (thanks, pre-money option pool) after Series C, which is less than the employee option poolCapital intensity makes it worse. If your company works with atoms (chips, robots, biotech), you burn two to three times the cash of a SaaS company and sell more of the company at every round. Jensen is the hardware founder's cautionary tale: decades of capital-hungry growth, and nothing left to vote with when it counted.The lesson: you don't lose control when the board votes. You lose it, one term sheet at a time, years before.Case Study: Apple and the Prodigal SonEvery founder knows this story, and every founder assumes it couldn't happen to them.In 1985, Steve Jobs was 30, a co-founder of Apple, and the person most responsible for its products and culture. He had no super-voting shares. The Macintosh launched to great reviews and disappointing sales. Jobs's "my way or the highway" style wore everyone out. John Sculley, the Pepsi executive Jobs had personally recruited with the famous "sugar water" pitch, moved to take away his operating authority.Jobs tried to get Sculley removed instead. The plan leaked, the board backed Sculley, and Jobs, with no structural power at all, resigned and went off to start NeXT.What followed was a twelve-year slide that brought Apple to within about 90 days of insolvency in 1997. The board, out of options, bought NeXT, mostly to get Jobs back. You know the rest: iMac, iPod, iPhone, and the most valuable company on Earth.Dual-class advocates like to say that if Jobs had held super-voting stock, Apple would have skipped a lost decade.Maybe. I'll give you the more uncomfortable version. The Jobs who got fired was probably not the Jobs who saved Apple. NeXT and Pixar humbled him and taught him things, and he came back a better CEO. Getting fired may have been the most valuable thing that ever happened to him, though it's hard to see it that way while it's happening.The Counter-Lesson: WeWork, or What Happens When Nobody Can Say NoAdam Neumann got the thing Jobs never had: . The board couldn't fire him, investors couldn't overrule him, and he ran the company accordingly.He bought buildings personally and leased them back to WeWork. He trademarked the word "We" and had his own company pay him for it. (He reversed that after the public backlash, which is a bit like returning the cookie once your mom has already seen the crumbs.)When the S-1 came out in August 2019, public investors saw $47 billion in lease obligations against $4 billion in committed revenue, plus governance that made Apple's 1985 board look like the Federalist Papers. The IPO collapsed and SoftBank had to fund a bailout. Neumann was out, and in 2023 the company filed for Chapter 11.Here's the lesson I care about most. Super-voting stock does two things: it protects you from the market's panic, and it protects you from your own mistakes. The first is valuable. The second can kill the company. The same structure that would have saved 1985 Jobs from Sculley also saved Neumann from anyone who might have told him no.So what should you actually do? Here is the playbook, roughly by stage. If you can, negotiate these terms when you have leverage, which means you need the money.Founder-friendly charter from day one. Authorizing a high-vote Class B institutional money arrives is far easier than recapitalizing later. Musk said he wanted 25% voting control at Tesla and admitted that retrofitting dual-class after the IPO is close to impossible. Don't put yourself in that position.Clean vesting and 83(b) elections. These are boring and they are essential.Board composition is the real cap table. Lock in seats elected by common stockholders. A 2-1-2 board (two founders, one independent, two VCs) holds up much better than a board where you have one seat and keep telling yourself the independent director is on your side.Supermajority to fire the CEO. Make your own termination without cause require a supermajority of the board. That gives you a veto over your own exit. The 2026 NVCA baseline lets a majority of preferred force a sale. Push for a (preferred common) and a , so you can't be forced to sign a deal in which the liquidation preferences consume everything and common gets nothing. These let you take some money off the table in a later round without giving up voting control. A founder who can pay the mortgage makes better long-term decisions.Dual-class with a sunset you choose. Glass Lewis and ISS now recommend voting against directors at companies that IPO without a time-based sunset. Pick your own, seven to ten years, before someone picks one for you.Choose your jurisdiction deliberately. Delaware's new Section 122(18) makes founder consent rights in stockholder agreements enforceable again after . Texas offers friendlier rules for controllers and has a growing business court. (See: Tesla's move after .)Character is part of your governance. No structure would have protected Jensen this week. Nvidia's code of conduct, the national-security issues, and lawmakers demanding briefings would have overridden any share class. Super-voting stock doesn't protect you from regulators, prosecutors, or your own direct reports.The Balance: Governance as Seatbelt, Not LeashThe academics have a useful framework for this. are the damage a founder does when nobody can stop them; that's WeWork. are the damage investors do when they're in charge: panic, short-termism, and a buyback where an R&D budget should be. That's 1985 Apple.Law professors Zohar Goshen and Richard Squire argue the right structure of the two. A visionary founder in a 20-year bet like AI, VR, or rockets should get more insulation. A mature company with a founder who has drifted should get less.The data supports this. Dual-class firms trade at a at IPO, because markets value the founder's vision. Around later, that premium tends to become a discount as the founder's economic stake shrinks while their votes don't.So the goal isn't maximum control. It's control that fits where your company is in its life: enough insulation to make long-term bets, with a working mechanism for someone to say "stop" if you lose your way.Jensen had plenty of the first and none of the second, which was fine for 33 years until this week. Neumann had too much of both. Jobs had none, and it took a lost decade to fix.Here's what I expect over the next five years.1. The Jensen effect on fundraising. Founders raising in 2027 will bring up Nvidia in every board-composition negotiation, and investors will bring up WeWork. Both are fair points.2. Trust-based structures as the new middle ground. Anthropic's S-1 shows a new model. The founders hold a Class F share that gives them 50.1% of ordinary votes, while an independent with no economic stake elects a majority of the board. The founders control the shareholder vote, and the trust controls the board. OpenAI's foundation keeps exclusive power over its PBC's board even though Microsoft owns 27% of the equity. These are deliberate checks and balances in a company charter, and you'll see others copy them.3. Sunsets become standard. Perpetual founder control is ending. Index providers, proxy advisors, and institutional investors all agree on that. Expect seven-to-ten-year sunsets to become the price of a dual-class IPO.4. The jurisdiction wars continue. Delaware vs. Texas vs. Nevada. Your state of incorporation is now a strategic decision, not a box your lawyer checks.5. Character as a governance mechanism. This is the uncomfortable one. As founders gain more structural protection, the remaining risks come from conduct: personal behavior, conflicts of interest, national security. Those risks don't care how many votes your shares carry.My closing advice to every engineer-founder reading this:Fight for control early, when it's cheap. Protect it with structure, not just goodwill. Give it an expiration date before someone else does. And above all, build a company and a character that a board would never want to fire.Jensen Huang built one of the greatest companies in history and still lost it in a week. Your share structure can't fully protect you from yourself, so you'll have to manage that part on your own.

item.title: Claude Merged 30,401 Changes in One Day. Git Couldn't Keep Up.
item.author: Sidra Zafar
item.content:encoded: An agent gets a task - fix a flaky test. Before it reads a single line of code, it needs a working copy of the repository.Under git, that meant waiting 7.1 minutes.Multiply that wait by tens of thousands of agents a day and you get the problem Anthropic described in its engineering post on 13 October 2026. The code wasn't the slow part any more. Claude could write the fix in seconds; the plumbing built for human engineers (source control, builds, CI) couldn't hand it the repo fast enough.So Anthropic threw out git for its main repository and built Scion.January: about 1,000 merges a dayThe numbers tell the story better than I can. In January 2026, Anthropic merged roughly 1,000 code changes a day. By May it was about 2,500.The team tried everything git offers to cope: shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, repository snapshots and several hundred git mirrors. Each one bought time. None of them bought enough, because the main-branch history was close to 100 GB and the compressed working copy was over 25 GB. CI alone ran around 25 million checkouts a day.The mirrors eventually outgrew their disks. At that point you can split the monorepo (and lose speed) or rebuild source control. Anthropic picked the second option.9 September: 30,401 mergesBy September, Anthropic was merging more than 30,000 changes a day. The peak was 30,401 on 9 September. That's a 12x jump in four months, and most of it came from Claude.That's the day git stopped being a tool and became a ceiling.Scion looks more like Subversion than git, and Anthropic says so openly. Git assumes every client is a full copy of history that can work offline. Scion assumes the opposite: clients are always online, so the server does the heavy lifting.The stack has four layers:, the client that runs on a developer laptop or inside an agent's sandbox, one per machine, which shares cached objects across every job on that node, regional caches that sit between the machines and the source of truth, the authoritative layer, backed by Google Spanner and cloud storageAnthropic reports a cache hit rate above 99% at every tier. Almost nothing travels all the way to the servers.The unit of history changes too. A git commit points to a full tree. A Scion lists only the files that changed relative to its first parent, each with a content-addressed pointer to a compressed blob. The server works out trees, history and blame from those changesets when someone asks.Branches are discouraged, except for main and release branches. Creating a changeset never touches a branch; moving one is a single compare-and-swap on one Spanner row. That's why 30,000 merges a day don't trip over each other.How Claude ships a change on Scion, step by stepAnthropic's post doesn't publish a single runbook, so this is the flow pieced together from what the team described. Follow one agent and one flaky test.Step 1: Get a worktree in seconds. Claude asks for a working copy. It doesn't clone anything. The client names the root tree it wants and fetches only the objects it's missing, usually from the local daemon. Checkouts are sparse or virtual: a file lands on disk only when Claude opens it. A new agent worktree went from 7.1 minutes to 5.1 seconds, an 84x speedup.Step 2: Ask the server questions instead of the disk. Where was this test last changed? Who touched this function? Under git, Claude would run or over local history. Under Scion, history, blame and diffs are server queries exposed through an API. Many jobs never need a local repository at all; Anthropic says its automated bisect and revert pipelines wouldn't be practical at scale without this.Step 3: Edit, and let status stay cheap. Claude changes two files. The client watches the filesystem rather than rescanning the whole tree, so checking status for an agent fell from 4.3 seconds to under 0.2.Step 4: Commit straight to the server. A commit creates a changeset on the server, and it's visible everywhere at once. There's no push step and no packfile negotiation. An agent commit dropped from 18 seconds to 761 milliseconds.Step 5: Open a change request in Antique. Antique is Anthropic's new code review tool, built alongside Scion. Reviewers check the of a change, not every line. Semantic approval rules can tell a comment-only edit apart from one that touches sensitive logic, so the review effort goes where the risk is. Review moved to Antique between May and June 2026; by August almost every merged change went through it.Step 6: Merge without a global queue. Here's the part that surprised me. Anthropic dropped the old globally locked merge queue, because serialising 30,000 merges a day doesn't work. Changes merge concurrently. When two of them conflict, Claude repairs the conflict.Step 7: Test after merge, before deploy. With no queue holding everything back, the safety net moves later. Post-merge and pre-deploy testing catches what pre-merge serialisation used to. If something breaks, the same cheap server-side history powers the automated bisect and revert.Add it all up and the source-control overhead for one change request fell from 34 minutes to 3.7 minutes. Across roughly 22,000 change requests a day, that's a lot of machine time handed back.The part Claude built itselfThere's a loop in this story I find hard to ignore. Claude created the load that broke git, and then Claude helped build the replacement.Engineers set the architecture, the scaling targets and the invariants. Claude wrote much of the code; the source control and Antique directories received 12,257 changes between January and September. The team's original git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline was hand-written. They gave it to an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview and asked for a rewrite, with no further instructions. The new version used 20x less memory and ran 4x faster, and it kept the ordering rules the old one relied on.The team also runs dedicated Claude instances that each watch one component's telemetry and logs (the daemon, the cache, Antique's merge flow). And the engineers' most common job, by their own account, was telling Claude "no"; for example, when it read the commit log instead of querying the review tool.Scion isn't free. You lose offline work: no server, no source control. You also lose portability, because Scion only makes sense with Anthropic's own review, search and CI systems wired around it.The results, as Anthropic reports them on its own workload:Source control per change requestThe infrastructure footprint shrank about 200x compared with the git mirror fleet, and CI needed 25% less CPU. These aren't general benchmarks against git, and Anthropic is careful to say so.You can't. Scion isn't open source, and Anthropic calls it "by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use."What it does want is for git platforms to borrow the ideas: full server-side APIs, a better fetch protocol, and stronger sparse and shallow support for agent-sized workloads. It credits Google's Piper, Meta's Sapling and the Mononoke server (with its Bonsai data model) for many of the techniques.If your team runs a handful of agents, git is fine. If you're heading toward thousands, look at where your agents spend their first seven minutes.That's where Anthropic found 30,000 merges a day.Sources: Anthropic Engineering, "Redesigning source control at Anthropic" (13 October 2026, updated 15 October); coverage by InfoQ, Simon Willison and Matthews Wong. All performance figures are company-reported.

item.title: The Psychology of Luxury Marketing: Why We Pay More for Less
item.author: yuna
item.content:encoded: Have you ever looked at a piece of bent metal and thought, “Why does this cost as much as a decent used car?”Recently, I stumbled across a Ferrari metal collar online. It cost . It looked like someone picked up a sheet of basic aluminum, bent it aggressively, painted it red, and said, “Yep, that’ll be two grand and a half, please.”It made me genuinely sit down and ask: Why the fuck would anyone pay that?Well, welcome to a niche little world called luxury marketing, which apparently means we add a ridiculous price tag to ordinary items and watch everyone scramble to buy them.Luxury marketing has three main pillars that conveniently work together to gaslight you into thinking that a tiny bottle of perfume = a down payment for a prime city apartment is a completely reasonable thing to pay for.The three main pillars of luxury marketing are: I know those sound like really scary terms, but trust me, I’m going to hold your hand and explain how they collectively gaslight you.I’m not a marketing person. All of this has come from research papers and articles I’ve read, plus whatever marginal bits I actually understood from them. 😭)When you think something you want is about to sell out, you’re more likely to impulsively buy it, even if you haven’t stopped to think about the pros and cons yet. You see something you like, notice that there is very little stock left, and suddenly you’re buying it without thinking about whether you actually need it or not.That’s essentially what the illusion of scarcity is: less availability, more wanting, quicker decisions, more impulsive buying, more urgency, and ultimately, more sales.→ What is the Illusion of Scarcity?The illusion of scarcity refers to the tactic of creating a perception that a product or service is in limited supply when, in reality, it might not be.It plays on the psychological principle that people are more likely to desire something they believe is running out or hard to obtain.FOMO [Fear of Missing Out]It compels people to take action when they believe they might miss out on something valuable or desirable.The illusion of scarcity uses this fear to make customers more likely to buy to avoid the regret of missing out.People are more motivated by the prospect of avoiding loss rather than gaining something.The illusion of scarcity creates a sense of potential loss. Consumers fear losing the opportunity to purchase the product or service. This fear of loss motivates consumers more than the desire to gain, pushing them to act quickly.When a consumer sees that a product is in limited stock or others are purchasing it quickly, they are more likely to believe the product is valuable and worth buying. The perception is reinforced by the idea that if others are scrambling to buy it, it must be worth having.(Shameless advertisement: I talk more about this in my July edition, where I talked about how Red Bull used this tactic in the trash can myth. For more info, click here — July Edition.)In luxury marketing, people aren’t just buying the product; they are buying the perceived social status that the said product provides them with.In emerging markets (such as the BRIC nations, i.e., Brazil, Russia, India, and China), it was observed that logo-flashy or more easily recognised luxury goods are more widely sought after by people, as they felt the need to separate themselves from the masses and perceive a higher social status, like Look at me, I am richer as compared to you, which is why I am higher on the social ladder as compared to you and make themselves stand out.Meanwhile, mature markets (such as the United States, Italy, and France) were observed to be moving towards more subtle, less flashy luxury items which aren’t very easily recognisable by someone who doesn’t know about it because they tend to do it for (so-called) internalised-luxury consumption. The term refers to the perception of purchasing luxury goods for themselves or to express themselves better and to integrate themselves into a certain social group.Mature market, in the above context, refers to markets that have reached a certain equilibrium and are characterised by modest growth.An emerging market, in the above context, refers to markets that have a chronic shortage of resources and are characterised by inadequate infrastructure but also yield impressive economic growth.So, in mature markets, people are moving towards a more subtle display of luxury, such as minimalistic or no logos, or a higher emphasis on the craftsmanship of the product. While emerging markets move more towards flashy, easily recognisable logos or/and patterns.Yet in general, both aren’t buying the product for the utilitarian purpose of the product, but rather are purchasing the product or service to display a certain social status and separate themselves from the masses, such as: I am different from you; I have a higher perceived social status than you; and I’m richer than you, and I have a certain expensiveness that you lack and am living a certain level of luxurious lifestyle that you cannot attain.Luxury marketing emphasizes the item's perceived social status. And consumers invest in it as they associate a certain sense of self-importance and a separation from the masses and their supposed (*air quotes*) superior social status with the ownership of the product, and therefore are willing to invest more in products that are marketed as a luxury, with the illusion of scarcity, than what might be the actual justified cost of the product solely based on utility if it wasn’t marketed as a luxury good or service.Heritage is a crucial part of a luxury brand, as it needs to have a modern aspect for the current society yet, at the same time, have a certain historical aspect to it.It adds an association of depth, authenticity, and credibility to the brand's perceived value and can result in increased brand loyalty and a willingness to accept higher prices.It marks within itself the strategic cultivation of the brand’s origins, traditions, and values over time. As Heritage builds on permanence, prestige, and authenticity, it gives luxury consumers a narrative and a mythology to associate themselves with, linking back to how they view their perceived social status increasing with consumption of luxury brands’ goods and/or services.

item.title: Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
The European Space Agency has released the largest dataset yet from its Euclid space telescope, containing 1.7 petabytes of observations covering more than 900 million galaxies. "The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth," reports Reuters. "The mission's goal is to complete the "largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031." From the report: "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales.
"Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. This will tell us where galaxies are in space and time, across 10 billion years, and in all directions beyond our galactic plane," Pettorino said. "Galaxies cluster along filaments, surrounded by empty space, and form a network that we call the cosmic web. Euclid will reconstruct the cosmic web and how it has grown over time. This is important because the exact configuration of the cosmic web, how many clusters or voids are there, how fast it changed, depend on the properties of dark energy and dark matter," Pettorino said.
[...] Previous Euclid data releases covered only a few days of observations. The newly released dataset includes more than a year of data and still spans only 14% of the total sky area Euclid is due to survey in visible and near-infrared light over six years. This data release will be completed next year with the first results on dark energy and dark matter.

item.title: SpaceX To Invest $74 Billion Into Data Center Construction Projects In Texas, Arizona
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from the Hill: Elon Musk's SpaceX plans to invest more than $74 billion into building two data centers in Texas and Arizona, the company announced Thursday, marketing them as projects that will boost local communities amid backlash surrounding such facilities. "These investments will expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create economic opportunities that extend far beyond the facilities themselves," the company said in a release. SpaceX said it will put more than $24 billion into a new project in Texas's Rio Grande Valley, expanding the company's headquarters in Starbase -- a coastal town the tech giant established in 2025 in a previously unincorporated area of Cameron County. In Arizona, SpaceX will invest around $50 billion in Cochise County, a rural area east of Tucson bordering Mexico and New Mexico.
SpaceX pledged the new projects will be created cooperatively with the surrounding communities and will be environmentally conscious. The company said the project in Texas would generate its own power and invest $220 million to expand the water supply in nearby Brownsville. While in Arizona, it vowed to work with local electric cooperatives and "potentially" reduce electric bills, saying the site would use dry cooling without water consumption. "They require strong partnerships with local communities, responsible environmental stewardship, and stable, competitive policies that give companies the confidence to make long-term investments," the company said in a release. Both sites promise hundreds of permanent jobs even once construction is complete.
